canonical_sources.title: Great Fire of London (consulted 2026-11-02; secondary summary of Tinniswood, Porter, Field, Hanson)
The Monument to the Great Fire of London

pedagogy.problem_statement: A city built largely of timber, and a spark in one bakery.
pedagogy.core_thesis: The fire began in one bakery, destroyed a large part of the old City, and prompted rebuilding in brick and stone.
pedagogy.mental_model: A story told as paper being assembled, then burned away, then rebuilt as a different material.
pedagogy.key_takeaway: London's brick-and-stone rebuilding was a response to the fire, and the fire's human cost is still uncertain.
verified_claims: A short time after midnight on Sunday 2 September 1666 a fire broke out at Thomas Farriner's bakery in Pudding Lane [Wikipedia, citing Tinniswood].
The fire ran from Sunday 2 to Wednesday 5 September 1666; the wind dropped on Tuesday evening and firebreaks took effect on Wednesday [Wikipedia, citing Tinniswood, Field].
An estimated 13,200-13,500 houses were destroyed [Wikipedia, citing Porter, Tinniswood, Field].
86 or 87 parish churches were destroyed, and St Paul's Cathedral was destroyed [Wikipedia, citing Porter, Tinniswood, Field].
The recorded death toll is traditionally very few (six is the traditional figure) and is disputed; some historians argue for far more [Wikipedia, citing Tinniswood, Porter, Hanson, Field].
The Rebuilding of London Act 1666 banned wood from building exteriors; rebuilt buildings were required to be brick and stone [Wikipedia, citing Field].
Christopher Wren rebuilt St Paul's Cathedral [Wikipedia].
The Monument is 202 ft (61.5 m) tall, designed by Wren and Robert Hooke, built 1671-1676 [themonument.org.uk for height and designers; Wikipedia for dates].
anti_patterns: Do not present any single death toll as established fact
Do not claim the Monument's height equals its distance from the bakery (not verified in the consulted sources)
Do not show generated or procedural imagery as archival material
Do not state a percentage of the City destroyed (the consulted source gives only a share of housing, with unclear base)
